note: One of the most argued openings in the poem. Aurora, the dawn, was the wife of Tithonus, and Dante calls this one his concubine. Most modern readers take her as a second, lesser dawn: the glow of the moon rising over Purgatory about three hours after sunset. Others take it as sunrise in Italy at the same moment.
Tithonus, a prince of Troy loved by Aurora, goddess of the dawn. She won him eternal life but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he grew older forever. Each morning she rises from his bed.
The stars of Scorpio, on the eastern horizon where the glow appears. A few readers argue for Pisces, the cold-blooded Fish.
The steps are usually taken as hours. Night began at about six, so two hours have gone and the third is nearly over: it is close to nine in the evening.

context: What Dante has from Adam is a body. Of the five in the valley, he alone is alive and needs sleep.

note: Dante, Virgil, Sordello, Nino Visconti and Currado Malaspina.

A myth from Ovid's Metamorphoses. King Tereus raped his wife's sister Philomela and cut out her tongue. The sisters took a terrible revenge, and all three were turned into birds. In the version Dante seems to follow, Philomela became the swallow.
A common ancient and medieval belief: dreams that come just before dawn tell the truth. Dante has three such dreams on the mountain, one on each night (here, and in Purgatorio 19 and 27).
The bird of Jupiter, and the emblem of the Roman Empire. The dream turns into images what is really happening to the sleeper, as Virgil explains below.

A Trojan prince, the most beautiful of mortals. He was hunting with his friends on Mount Ida, near Troy, when Jupiter's eagle carried him off to be cupbearer to the gods. The "high assembly" is their council.
Medieval science placed a layer of pure fire above the air and below the moon. Flames rise because they are trying to get back to it.

context: His mother, the sea goddess Thetis, wanted to keep him from the Trojan War. She took him asleep from his tutor, the centaur Chiron, to the island of Scyros and hid him there dressed as a girl. The story is told in the Achilleid of Statius.

note: Ulysses and Diomedes tricked Achilles into giving himself away. It is one of the deceits they pay for in Inferno 26.
After eight in the morning on Easter Monday.

context: Purgatory itself, at last. Everything below this cliff was only the waiting place.
She was the eagle of the dream. Dante dreamed of being seized and burned; in truth he was carried gently, asleep, up a slope he could not have climbed.

note: Lucia is the saint of eyesight. She shows the way with her eyes and says nothing.
Another direct word to the reader. The entry into Purgatory is a higher subject, and Dante says his writing will rise to meet it. The scene that follows is the most carefully built allegory so far.
The gate works like the sacrament of confession, and the steps are usually read as its three parts: owning up to one's sins, sorrow for them, and making amends. Readers differ on which step is which.
An angel who acts as a priest hearing confession. No one enters Purgatory without passing him.
Usually read as God's justice, or as the judgment a confessor must use.
Souls normally come here on their own. As at the foot of the mountain in Canto 1, the guardian wants to know by what right these two have come.
Lucia. Her name is the password.
Most often read as honest self-examination and confession: the sinner sees himself as he truly is, as in a mirror.
Most often read as contrition. The word comes from the Latin for crushed: the hard heart is broken, and the cracks form a cross.
A hard, deep red stone used for the tombs of emperors. The blood-red step is read as the love that drives a penitent to make amends, or as the blood of Christ, which pays for sin.
The hardest of stones. It is read as the firmness a confessor needs, or as the rock on which Christ said he would build his Church.
The gesture of the Latin prayer of confession, made at the words "through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault".

P for peccatum, Latin for sin. The seven marks stand for the seven deadly sins: pride, envy, wrath, sloth, avarice, gluttony and lust. Each of the mountain's seven terraces cleanses one, and an angel wipes one P away as Dante leaves it.
The color of penance and humility. The angel with the dazzling face wears the plainest robe in the poem: a priest hears confession as a servant, not a lord.
The keys of the kingdom of Heaven, which Christ promised to Peter in Matthew's Gospel. Crossed, one gold and one silver, they are the emblem of the popes.

The gold key is the power to forgive sins, which cost Christ's death. The silver key is the confessor's judgment: he must first work out whether the sinner is truly sorry. That takes skill, and it is used first.

context: His instruction to the angel is to lean toward mercy: better to let in one too many than to shut out anyone who kneels.

note: To look back is to turn again toward the old life. It recalls Lot's wife, who looked back at Sodom and became a pillar of salt, and Christ's saying that no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

The Tarpeian rock on the Capitol in Rome, where the state treasury was kept. The poet Lucan describes the rock roaring when its doors were forced. The gate of Purgatory grinds just as loudly, because it opens so seldom.
A Roman tribune. In 49 BC, when Julius Caesar marched into Rome and went to seize the treasury, Metellus stood in the doorway and had to be dragged aside.
"We praise you, God": the Church's great Latin hymn of thanksgiving, sung on days of rejoicing. Here it greets a soul coming in.
The words come and go under the music. The singing may also be drowned in part by the roar of the hinges.
